questions.passage: Spoons are indispensable eating utensils in our daily lives. Throughout history, spoons have been made of different materials for different purposes, but they typically consist of a small bowl-shaped part with a long handle. According to archeological discoveries,the invention of spoons canbe traced back to 1,oooBC, during which ancient Egyptians are said to have first made spoons out of wood,flint and ivory for ornamental and religious purposes. Back then, spoons, as a symbol of wealth, were in the possession of Egyptian priests and Pharaohs. These ancient Egyptian spoons had elaborate drawings and hieroglyphic descriptions of religious events on their handles and bowls. In ancient Greece and the Roman Empire, spoons were frequently produced with higher value materials like bronze or silver and became more common among upper classes. The earliest mentioning of spoon in England can be traced back to 1259, in KingEdward I'swardrobe accounts. Coronation of everykingof England involved the use of special spoons adorned with tiny pearls.Upon the dawn of medieval Europe, spoons were crafted in horns, wood, and brass as a means of eating for both people and animals. Not until the 15"h century were wooden spoons replaced by more durable metal ones.Eventually,by the late1700s,spoons transformed intothe modernonesweknowtoday. In modern times, spoons are not only used for serving or eating food, but they also function as a tool for different tasks.The term“spoonfulis thus created to refer to the amount that a spoon can hold as a standard unit of measure in cooking. A teaspoon holds approximately 5 ml while a tablespoon measures three times the volume of a teaspoon.As for a dessertspoon,it is medium-sized,roughly equivalent to10 ml. Aside from measuring spoons, dozens of variations of spoons are designed for specific purposes. For example, special spoons are designed exclusivelyfor caviar.They are often made out of wood,gold, or animal horn because silver may changeits taste.In essence,the multiplefunctions and designs of spoons reflecttheirindispensablerolein ourlives.

questions.passage: Doyoulike towear a sweatshirt?Whenyou wear it,haveyou ever looked down andnoticed a small triangle 21 right below the neck? And have you ever wondered why it's there? Though a fashion statement today,this triangle,known as the V-notch,22 some practical purposes when the sweatshirt was invented a century ago. In the 1920s, Benjamin Russell Jr.,a quarterback for a football team, was upset about the constant itching caused by the team's wool football uniforms. Seeking a more comfortable23,he partnered with his father, who owned the Russell Manufacturing Company. Together, they developed a thick cotton practice jersey that ensured both comfort and durability.Their24 eventuallyledtothecreationofa new division: the Russell Athletic Company, dedicated solely to sweatshirt production. TheV-notchhasremainedone featureof thesweatshirt sinceitsintroductionbyRussell Athletic in 1926. Though it may appear purely decorative today, the V-notch was originally a functional 26.The design made it easier for thewearer to slipon the sweatshirt.Asthewearergets theirhead through the neck of the sweatshirt, the V-notch would stretch to27.Also, since the chest is a major point of perspiration, the thicker cotton panel of the V-notch could help absorb28,keeping athletes dry during intense physical activity. Over time, the V-notch continues to29 its presence though sweatshirts have evolved from athletic gear into everyday casual wear. It may appear30today, but its existence adds a touch of old-school charm tomodernsweatshirts,giving each pieceanelevated look.Sonext timeyouwearyour favorite sweatshirt, you've got to appreciate this significant design. questions.stem: Whatisthemainideaofthearticle?
option_texts: The influence of Chinese cuisine onJapanese food.
A detailed look at funazushi,an ancient form of sushi.
The popularity of sushi in high-end restaurants.
questions.passage: When it comes to sushi, people usually think of mounds of rice with a slice of raw fish on top. However, the sushi we enjoy today is in fact totally different from what is considered the earliest and most primitive type of sushi,funazushi. Funazushi is essentially a kind of narezushi,which features fermented fish. The exact origin of narezushi is unknown, but it is widely believed that it originated in China and spread into Japan around the 8 century. Back when refrigerators were not yet invented, this practice of fermenting fish with salt or rice extended its shelf life,ensuring the dish remained nutritious and safe to eat.Later,funa fish,a freshwater fish often found in Japan's Lake Biwa, became the main ingredient of narezushi, thus the namefunazushi. Making traditional funazushi is a delicate and surprisingly time-consuming process. First, unwanted parts of fish, such as scales, gills and internal organs, are removed. Next, the fish is packed with salt and layered in a wooden tub,left to ferment in a cool, dark place for twoyears.After the first stage,each fish is thoroughly washedwithrunningwater,dried in the sunfor one day,and thenpickledwithricefor one more year. To enjoy it, simply slice the fish thinly or dip it in some soy sauce. The long fermentation processgives thefish a distinctlystrong and sour taste thatresemblesblue cheese.It may take a fewtries to get used to,but like many foods with strong flavors, the more you try, the more likely it is to grow on you. Today, while the modern “fast-food” version of sushi we are eating now enjoys widespread popularity, fewer and fewer people are making funazushi. Because of this, funazushi has become a luxury food only found in traditional or high-end Japanese restaurants, often served in various creative ways. Thousands of years have passed,but no matter how sushi has evolved,funazushi’s fermentation process continues,lying at theheartof Japan's culinaryculture.

questions.passage: Have you ever heard people talk about a past event,only to learn that their memories differ from the actual facts?Thisphenomenon isknown as theMandelaEffect.The termwascoinedbyFionaBroome, whonoticed that she and othersremembered NelsonMandela dyinginprisonduring the1980s,even thoughhe actuallypassed away in 2013after serving asSouthAfrica's president. These shared false memories have long fascinated both scientists and the general public. Psychologistsbelieve theMandelaEffect stemsfrom thewayhumanmemoryworks.Instead of storing perfect copies of events, our brains reconstruct memories using fragments of information and prior expectations. Psychologists often explain this using two main ideas:“source monitoring error” and "schema theory." A source monitoring error occurs when people misremember where a memory originated.For example,they might think they saw something on the newswhen they actually heard about it in a conversation. Schema theory, on the other hand, suggests that the brain fills gaps with familiarpatterns,sometimesproducingfalsememoriesthatfeel entirelyreal. Onewell-knownexampleoftheMandelaEffectcomesfromachildren'sbookseriescalled The Berenstain Bears.Many people recall the name spelled as“Berenstein,”with“-stein”being a more common spelling in English. However, the correct spelling has always been “Berenstain." Our brain might unconsciouslychange the memorytomatch more familiar patterns. This widespread misremembering,shared by thousands ofreaders,shows how false memories can influence groups,not just individuals. Somepeoplepropose more imaginative theories to explain theMandela Effect.One involves parallel universessuggestingtheremaybeotherversionsofourworldwhere eventsunfoldeddifferently. According to this theory,thosewhoexperience theMandelaEffectmayhavememoriesfrom another universe.Whilenot supported byscientific evidence,this idea is often exploredinfiction andhighlights how mysterious memory—and the universe—can be. mirror onthewall".

questions.stem: What does the first paragraph mainly suggest?
option_texts: People like to hoard useless items.
Hoarding is more than just owning many things.
questions.passage: Look around your living space. Do you see items you haven't used in years? Old clothes, expired longer than they should, but for some, this habit can become overwhelming and turn into a serious problem. They hoard, acquiring an excessive number of items, and store them in a chaotic manner. Psychologists suggest that hoarding often stems from a deep emotional attachment to objects, a fear of waste, or the belief that an item might be useful in the future. Unaware of these emotional factors, uncontrollable cycle of collecting. The difference between thoughtful saving and compulsive accumulation is subtle. Meanwhile, today's consumer culture constantly encourages people to buy more. Sales promotions, advertising, and social media all fuel the idea that possessions equal happiness. Such an implication rids people of the guilt of spending beyond their needs. It's easy to see why people fall for it. Nevertheless, as their homes fill up with things they don't need, excessive belongings can weigh on both their living spaces and their minds. In more extreme cases, hoarding can be linked to past trauma, with control. Studies estimate that around 2 to 6% of the population struggles with compulsive hoarding out of emotional or societal pressures, and many cases go unreported. When hoarding is severe, it can lead to physical or psychological harm to hoarders and their families, resulting in sanitation issues, strained relationships, or unsafe living conditions. For example, in one case, a woman in New York was found living in a home so packed with possessions that emergency responders couldn't enter. In another, a man's hoarding problem led to public danger, as piles of paper and garbage posed a fire hazard in his apartment. While hoarding may begin with innocent intentions—saving money, preserving memories, or avoiding waste—it can spiral into something much more serious. Recognizing the signs and understanding the emotional roots of hoarding is the first step toward change.

questions.stem: Which of the following pictures best depicts a pika?
questions.passage: Pikas, rodent-like creatures belonging to the family Ochotonidae within the order Lagomorpha, are small, mountain-dwelling mammals found in Asia and North America. Measuring approximately 15 centimeters in length and weighing between 125 and 200 grams, they are characterized by their dark bead-like eyes, rounded ears, lack of an external tail, and soft, dense fur. Unlike their lagomorph relatives—rabbits and hares, pikas have shorter hind limbs, resulting in a brisk scurry rather than bounding leaps when they move around. Adapted to cold, alpine environments, pikas inhabit rocky slopes and meadows at elevations reaching up to 6,ooo meters. They are active in the daytime, especially during cooler parts of the day. Notably, pikas do not hibernate, and they prepare for winter by creating “haypiles"collections of dried vegetation such as grasses, flowers, and twigs—which they store under rocks or in crevices for sustenance during the colder months. Their diet primarily consists of various plant materials, including leaves, stems, seeds, and occasionally bark. Pikas exhibit coprophagy, which is a common trait among lagomorphs. They have two types of droppings: hard pellets and soft cecotropes, and they consume the latter once again to extract additional nutrients. Pikas’ reproductive and social behaviors have also fascinated scientists. Reproduction occurs in the spring, with females typically producing two to six offspring per litter after carrying them for about 30 ss within 40 to 50 days. Social structures among pikas vary by species and habitat. Rock-dwelling species tend to be solitary and territorial, using vocalizations to communicate and defend their areas.In contrast, burrowing species often live in family groups, exhibiting more social behaviors. Pikas are not just survivors of high-altitude lifethey are vital indicators of ecosystem health. Their alpine regions. As temperatures rise, pikas are forced to retreat to higher elevations or face local extinction, highlighting the urgency of preserving their habitats. Humans need to put more effort into conservation to ensure that theseremarkable creatures continue to thrive in their mountainous homes.

questions.passage: In a remote village surrounded by jagged hills, life unfolded in simple yet arduous ways. The villagers shared a strong bond, yet their lives were dictated by their harsh environment. Narrow dirt paths wound precariously through rocky terrain,making obtaining even the most basic necessities a daily struggle. There, distance was not merely a measure of kilometers; rather, it was an invisible wall, cutting them off from the possibilities of another world. Amid the mountains stood a man named Dashrath Manjhi, unaware that his life would later be transformed. One day, his wife perished in a dreadful accident on the perilous trail leading to the village. Overwhelmed with sorrow, he resolved to carve a passage through the stone barriers to reach the more prosperous towns beyond. He told people about his strong ambition, but he was soon dismissed by those around him as a madman for embarking on an impossible mission. Nevertheless, Manjhi took up a hammer and a chisel, vowing to confront the mountains that had long controlled the villagers’ fate. Day after day, year after year, he fought bravely against the unyielding monster, enduring monsoon rains and the blistering sun. Selling his few goats to buy tools, he worked morning and evening—before and after his day job as a laborer. After twenty-two relentless years, the road he carved shrank the distance between isolation and opportunity from fifty kilometers to ten. His feat earned him the title of "Mountain Man,” and the path he created became known as a monument of love, drawing tourists and admirationfromacrosstheworld. Yet, beneath the huge reverence lies a quiet irony. While his story inspired films and memorials, Manjhi's family still live in poverty, struggling as wage laborers in the very village his labor transformed. The movie about his life earned praise and profit, but his descendants reportedly received only a meager payment from the filmmakers—barely enough to build a house. Perhaps the true mountain was not the one he carved through, but the indifference of a society quick to praise a legend, yet slow to uplift the livesleftbehind their life. from the outsideworld.

The villagers shared a strong bond, yet their lives were dictated by their harsh environment. Narrow dirt paths wound precariously through rocky terrain,making obtaining even the most basic necessities a daily struggle. There, distance was not merely a measure of kilometers; rather, it was an invisible wall, cutting them off from the possibilities of another world. Amid the mountains stood a man named Dashrath Manjhi, unaware that his life would later be transformed. One day, his wife perished in a dreadful accident on the perilous trail leading to the village. Overwhelmed with sorrow, he resolved to carve a passage through the stone barriers to reach the more prosperous towns beyond. He told people about his strong ambition, but he was soon dismissed by those around him as a madman for embarking on an impossible mission. Nevertheless, Manjhi took up a hammer and a chisel, vowing to confront the mountains that had long controlled the villagers’ fate. Day after day, year after year, he fought bravely against the unyielding monster, enduring monsoon rains and the blistering sun. Selling his few goats to buy tools, he worked morning and evening—before and after his day job as a laborer. After twenty-two relentless years, the road he carved shrank the distance between isolation and opportunity from fifty kilometers to ten. His feat earned him the title of "Mountain Man,” and the path he created became known as a monument of love, drawing tourists and admirationfromacrosstheworld. Yet, beneath the huge reverence lies a quiet irony. While his story inspired films and memorials, Manjhi's family still live in poverty, struggling as wage laborers in the very village his labor transformed. The movie about his life earned praise and profit, but his descendants reportedly received only a meager payment from the filmmakers—barely enough to build a house. Perhaps the true mountain was not the one he carved through, but the indifference of a society quick to praise a legend, yet slow to uplift the livesleftbehind their life. from the outsideworld.
